Lessons.Title: Graphing Linear Inequalities in Two Variables (Part 1)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: test ordered pairs against a two-variable inequality, identify the boundary line and half-plane of solutions and distinguish inclusive from strict inequalities. Original Edulytiks adaptation based on Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U02:L21, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/21/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). The source's primary activity plots solutions and non-solutions to discover the correct region, not just labels a prepared graph.

Original comparison 2x+3y≤12 in the real coordinate plane. The boundary line 2x+3y=12 has intercepts (6,0) and (0,4). Solving for y gives y≤4−(2/3)x, so shade below the line. The boundary is solid because equality satisfies ≤; for 2x+3y<12 it would be dashed.

Point (0,5) gives 15>12, so outside; (3,1) gives 9≤12, so inside; (0,4) gives 12, so on and included. Point (−1,−1) gives −5≤12, hence also inside the mathematical half-plane. Do not assume x or y must be positive unless the application context adds that restriction.

Student task: independently create the line and plot at least four solutions and four non-solutions, distinguish the solid/dashed boundary, and exchange explanations. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): correct boundary and intercepts, accurate point classification, correct shading and inequality symbol, and justified graphic interpretation with accessible text.

KeyConcepts.Title: Boundary line
KeyConcepts.Definition: Replace inequality symbol with = to locate the separating straight line.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Find intercepts and check a point on it.

KeyConcepts.Title: Half-plane
KeyConcepts.Definition: A linear inequality in two real variables determines one side of its boundary.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Test a point not on the line to identify the shaded region.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inclusive boundary
KeyConcepts.Definition: ≤ and ≥ include equality boundary, while < and > exclude it.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use solid for included, dashed for excluded.

WorkedExamples.Title: Build a solution graph
WorkedExamples.Question: Graph 2x+3y≤12.
WorkedExamples.Method: Model the constraint, test boundary cases, and verify the original comparison.
Steps: At x=0, y=4; at y=0, x=6.
Test origin (0,0): 0≤12 true, so shade the side containing origin.
Use solid line because equality included.
WorkedExamples.Check: The origin is included and (0,5) excluded.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify three points
WorkedExamples.Question: Check (0,5),(3,1),(0,4) for 2x+3y≤12.
WorkedExamples.Method: Model the constraint, test boundary cases, and verify the original comparison.
Steps: At (0,4), value is 12≤12, true at boundary.
State included cases independently of any guess from the picture.

WorkedExamples.Title: Contrast strict and inclusive
WorkedExamples.Question: Is (6,0) a solution to ≤ but not <?
WorkedExamples.Method: Model the constraint, test boundary cases, and verify the original comparison.
Steps: Draw solid for first and dashed for second.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes; boundary belongs only to the non-strict inequality.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Shading the wrong side because of visual intuition

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A dashed line for ≤ loses valid equality solutions.

SummaryPoints: Graph related equality, then test a point to find the half-plane.
For 2x+3y≤12, intercepts are (6,0),(0,4) and region is below a solid line.
Negative coordinates can be algebraically valid even without a physical interpretation.
Teacher assesses actual graph construction and reasoning.
